quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn died 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County (tree fact F2, cited to S3, Pennsylvania Death Certificates). No assertion has been extracted from that certificate and the log has no search of it. Pennsylvania statewide certificates from 1906 usually name the decedent's father and mother, so this record can answer the parentage question directly. The Pennsylvania Death Certificates collection is name-searchable.

The 1850 census (log_001) places Patrick, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's household, but it does not state relationships (assertion a_004 is inferred from household position). The 1880 census is the first US census to record each person's relationship to the head, so it can show whether Patrick is listed as Thomas's son. The United States 1880 census is name-searchable.

Closes the 1851-1860 evidence gap in timeline t_001 (severity medium; the 1860 census is unsearched). It does not give relationships, but it shows whether Thomas Flynn's household still includes a boy of about 15 and whether its composition held, which supports or weakens the 1850 household link. The United States 1860 census is name-searchable.

Baptisms of Thomas Flynn's other children in Schuylkill parishes would name both parents, including the mother's given name, which no record in hand gives. The Pennsylvania Births and Christenings collection and the Schuylkill County church records are name-searchable. Catholic registers stayed with the Diocese of Philadelphia, so search the parish registers as indexed, then verify the originals with the parish. A sibling baptism would also identify Thomas's wife and the Catholic parish the family used.

Dedicated item for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (born about 1818, Ireland) to his wife, which should give the mother's maiden name if this was her first marriage. Thomas's marriage date is unknown, so the window runs from his likely marriageable age to shortly before Patrick's birth. The Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 and Pennsylvania Marriages 1709-1940 collections are name-searchable. The marriage shows the couple as a unit; it does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. Each marriage record for the wife should be checked if a remarriage is suspected.

If Thomas Flynn died while Patrick was a minor or young adult, his will or administration could name Patrick as a son and his wife by name. The window follows Thomas's own lifespan (born about 1818), not the 1850 census window. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of Schuylkill County Register of Wills dockets. The Thomas Flynn index should be searched by name first.

Burial records and cemetery listings for Thomas Flynn and Patrick Flynn may give death dates, ages and family links for both men. The Pennsylvania Cemetery Records collection is name-searchable. A burial entry for Patrick in 1908 would also be a second check on the death certificate in item 1.

Land deeds and wills in the Pennsylvania Wills and Deeds collection may name Thomas Flynn's wife (for example, in a dower release) and any sons who received property. The collection is name-searchable. This also tests whether the family held land that passed to Patrick.

FAN item. Records of the dwellings next to Thomas Flynn's household (dwelling 84 in the 1850 census, per the timeline) may show Irish families with shared surnames, witnesses, or kin, and so point to a candidate for Thomas's wife's family. This is a lead-generating item, not proof. The 1850 United States census is name-searchable.

If Thomas Flynn died in a census year's preceding year (1849-1880), the mortality schedules name him with age and place of death. Such a death would explain why he is absent from later census records. The United States Census Mortality Schedule collection is name-searchable. Search only if items 3, 5 and 6 leave Thomas's death date unresolved.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn died 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County. That death falls after statewide registration began in 1906, so a state death certificate should exist. The tree already attaches a Pennsylvania death certificate (S3), but its parent-name and informant fields are not yet read into the project. Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 is name-searchable and should be checked for the same certificate. Test whether it names the father (Thomas Flynn) and the mother, and who gave the information.

The 1880 United States census is name-searchable nationally and is the first census to record relationship to the head of household. The 1850 entry places Patrick (age 5, born Ireland) in Thomas Flynn's household, but 1850 states no relationship, so that link is still inferred. If Thomas is alive in 1880, a listing of Patrick as son of Thomas would test parentage directly. If Thomas is gone, the widow's household may still show Patrick as son and name the mother's first name.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.rationale: Primary research objective. The tree holds the couple and five children; no records have been searched yet for any others.

entry.rationale: The 1850 census is the first federal schedule that names every household member with age and birthplace. Its Greene County household for Thomas (about 1810, Pennsylvania) and Sarah should list all children at home in 1850, which may add children born before 1850 that the tree does not hold. The tree's five children (Mary about 1836, John about 1838, Rebecca about 1841, William about 1844, Joseph about 1847, all Greene County births) are the names to check against it. Name-searchable on FamilySearch (United States Census, 1850).

The 1860 census names each household member with age, sex and birthplace. It tests whether any child born after 1850 was in the household, and lists younger children whose birth years fall after the 1850 schedule. Name-searchable on FamilySearch (United States Census, 1860). The tree records Thomas as deceased by 1868, so the household is expected under Sarah's name only after his death.

The 1870 census lists the widowed Sarah (if living) and any children still at home after Thomas's 1868 death, with ages and birthplaces. It may also place a child not yet found in the 1850 or 1860 schedules. Name-searchable on FamilySearch (United States Census, 1870).

The 1840 census names only the head of household. Other members appear as unnamed tallies in age brackets, so this item does not name children. It counts the young children in Thomas's household to show whether children born about 1833-1835, before Mary (about 1836), were living there. Name-searchable on FamilySearch (United States Census, 1840) for the head only; the household tally must be read from the image.

Christening or baptism entries are the earliest direct naming of a child with both parents. They could show a child born before Mary (about 1836) or after Joseph (about 1847) that the tree lacks. Name-searchable on FamilySearch (Ohio, Births and Christenings, 1821-1962). A parish register would need the same search on its Greene County church.

Ohio county birth records from 1841 may name the father and mother for births after 1841, which covers the later children (Rebecca, William, Joseph) and any child born after Joseph. Earlier births before 1841 are outside this collection's range, so this item cannot rule out a child born about 1833-1840. Name-searchable on FamilySearch (Ohio, County Births, 1841-2003).

The marriage of Thomas Hale and Sarah fixes the earliest possible birth date for their children and may name Sarah's maiden name and the bond date. The tree holds no marriage fact for the couple. The marriage may have taken place in Pennsylvania, where Thomas was born, rather than Greene County. Greene County marriage records survive from 1803 per the locality guide. Name-searchable on FamilySearch (Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2016).

Thomas died in 1868 in Greene County per the tree. A death or burial entry may name survivors, the informant (often a widow or son) or the children's ages and residences. Name-searchable on FamilySearch (Ohio, Deaths and Burials, 1854-1997).

Thomas died in 1868, so his estate file, held by the Greene County Probate Court (the Court of Common Pleas before 1852 per the locality guide), should name the heirs, which is the most direct list of children. Probate collection is browse-only (Ohio, Probate Records, 1789-1996), so this is an image browse of the estate file, not a name search. The window is sized to the time an estate takes to settle after a 1868 death.

If Sarah died after 1868 and left an estate, her file names the surviving children as heirs. The window runs to 1900 because Sarah's death date is unknown and a widow born about 1810-1820 could have died much later. Browse-only (Ohio, Probate Records, 1789-1996). Sized to the widow's plausible lifespan, not the 1868 death.

John (about 1838), William (about 1844) and Joseph (about 1847) were of Civil War age, and a service record or the grave registration may name a parent and a family. This item tests whether the known sons appear and whether an unknown son did. Name-searchable on FamilySearch (Ohio, Military Discharge Records, 1834-2004). The window is set to the war years. Adjusted to fit the statewide collection.

The tree's five children (Mary about 1836, John about 1838, Rebecca about 1841, William about 1844, Joseph about 1847, all Greene County births) are the names to check against it. It tests whether any child born after 1850 was in the household, and lists younger children whose birth years fall after the 1850 schedule. The 1840 census names only the head of household. Other members appear as unnamed tallies in age brackets, so this item does not name children. It counts the young children in Thomas's household to show whether children born about 1833-1835, before Mary (about 1836), were living there. Name-searchable on FamilySearch (United States Census, 1840) for the head only; the household tally must be read from the image.

The marriage of Thomas Hale and Sarah fixes the earliest possible birth date for their children and may name Sarah's maiden name and the bond date. The tree holds no marriage fact for the couple. ## Baiersbronn, Württemberg - 1800s

Church books are on Archion (parish page above).

entry.rationale: Katharina's baptism, about 1843, is the entry most likely to name her father and mother together. The locality entry (loc_001) records that the Evangelische Kirche Baiersbronn registers are digitised on Archion, a paid site, not on FamilySearch, so this is a manual browse of the parish register at https://www.archion.de/de/alle-archive/baden-wuerttemberg/evangelisches-archiv-baden-und-wuerttemberg-wuerttemberg/dekanat-freudenstadt/baiersbronn. The register's start date is not recorded, so this item may find no entry; item 5 is its fallback.

The parents' marriage in the Evangelische Kirche Baiersbronn register, dated before Katharina's birth. It would give both parents' names and the mother's maiden name, which census and death records usually omit. It confirms the couple as a unit and corroborates a father named by other evidence, but by itself it does not show that Katharina is their child. Search the mother's name as it appears in any marriage entry, since she may have married more than once.

Full-sibling baptisms in the same parish register, naming the same father and mother. A baptism of a child who is clearly a sibling places Katharina with the parents in the household, which the marriage alone cannot do. This is the FAN and parentage item the question requires, and it supplies the link the marriage record cannot.

Katharina's own marriage entry. German Protestant marriage entries usually name the bride's parents and her birthplace, which gives a second, independent statement of her parentage and may confirm her origin if the baptism is not found.

Katharina's own death or burial entry, a fallback for item 1. Death and burial entries often state an age, a home parish or a parent's name, and they are the usual route to her origin when the baptism register does not reach back to her birth. The tree holds no death date for her, so the window is set from her marriage years onward and is open to revision.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: Patrick was born in Ireland (1850 and 1860 censuses), so his own baptism is outside the Pennsylvania records. Children of Thomas Flynn born after the family reached Pennsylvania should appear in a Schuylkill County Catholic register. The Pennsylvania Births and Christenings collection is name-searchable; a baptism naming Thomas Flynn as father, with the mother's name, would test the household and give the mother's name. Sibling baptisms naming the same parents are FAN evidence bearing directly on Patrick's parentage. Catholic registers are held by the parish or the Diocese of Philadelphia, so any indexed hit must be checked against the parish original.

Dedicated parents'-marriage item for Thomas Flynn (b. about 1818, Ireland). The Pennsylvania Church Marriages and County Marriages collections are both name-searchable for Schuylkill. The record would name the wife, give the mother's maiden name if this was her first marriage, and date the union against Patrick's birth about 1845. Search every Thomas Flynn marriage in the window, because the wife's maiden name is unknown and a remarriage is not excluded. If the couple married in Ireland before emigrating, that marriage is outside this locality and is not planned here.

Thomas Flynn's death and burial are not in the tree or the log, and the 1860 census is his last located household. Burial registers and cemetery records are name-searchable here and often give age, birthplace and a surviving wife's name. A Catholic burial entry would also pin his death year, which bounds the probate search in the next item. Mortality schedules for 1850-1880 are name-searchable and can be checked in the same pass.

Thomas Flynn's will or administration, held by the Schuylkill County Register of Wills; the parent-jurisdiction rule does not apply to this window. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the county's dockets for Flynn estates. A will or inventory naming Patrick as a son would be direct parentage evidence and would advance the proof summary from probable toward proved. The window runs from Thomas's plausible death ages (about 32 to 82, since he was born about 1818), not from the subject's life, because the creator's death year is unknown.

Fallback for the Register of Wills browse: the Pennsylvania Wills and Deeds collection is name-searchable and may index a will or estate filing that the probate image browse misses. Use if the Register of Wills dockets show no Flynn estate or the browse is too costly. Search by Thomas Flynn with Schuylkill as the place.

Land deeds for Thomas Flynn in the Wills and Deeds collection, which is name-searchable. A deed's boundary recital names adjoining landowners, who are neighbors and often kin, and a later deed may name heirs. This is FAN evidence for the Flynn household and a check on whether Thomas held land at all, which would be the origin of any estate filing.

Patrick Flynn's own marriage record. The County Marriages and Church Marriages collections are name-searchable. Some county marriage entries give the groom's parents, so the record may name Thomas Flynn and bear on whether Patrick was Thomas's son. Patrick's marriage is a separate item from the parents' marriage in the second item, and is not a substitute for it.

- pli_006: Marriage of Thomas Flynn and his wife, 1838-1848, Schuylkill County (FamilySearch, name-searchable collections). This is the parents' marriage and should name the mother. Each marriage of Thomas must be pulled, since a surname from one marriage is not proof of her birth name.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

The 1880 census is the one federal count between those points, so it shows whether he was already in the coal region before 1882, what he did there, his birthplace, and his relationship to the head of household. The collection is name-searchable. Civil registration did not start statewide until 1906, so this census is one of the few sources that can date his arrival.

The 1882 directory entry (log_002) lists Michael as a miner in Schuylkill County, but it was found incidentally and does not show when he arrived. Directories for the years on either side of 1882 show whether he appears in the county in 1880 or 1881, and at what town or occupation. The directory collection is name-searchable.

If Michael married in or near the coal region, his marriage entry gives his residence and occupation at the date of marriage, and the bride's home parish and family, which may place the household in the county before 1882. Michael's own marriage date is not in the tree. The statewide marriage collection is name-searchable, so this is a name search. A companion browse of the county marriage volume is the fallback.

Fallback for the marriage name search. Schuylkill County's marriage register for 1870-1910 is a browse-only image group, so the marriage entry must be read page by page if the name search does not find it. Same question as the item it backs up: where Michael lived and worked when he married.

Baptisms of any children born to Michael after 1882 were recorded in the Catholic parish where the family lived. The sacramental entry names the parish and sometimes the father's occupation, which places the household in the coal region by a dated act. Pre-1906 civil registration is absent, so church registers are the dated source for this household. The collection is name-searchable.

Fallback for the baptism name search. The county church records group is browse-only and covers 1842-1895 in English and German. Parish sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese, not the county, so the parish register image set is the route if the indexed entries are missing. Same question as the item it backs up.

Michael's own land purchase or mining-company lease, if any, is recorded in the county deed books kept by the Recorder of Deeds. Most coal-region laborers leased from mining companies rather than buying land, so the target is a lease or a deed to a company, not a purchase. The county deed group is browse-only (about one-fifth record-searchable), so the search is an image browse of Michael's surname index. A dated deed in the county would show he held property there by a given year.

Family and neighbour (FAN) item. Patrick Sheahan, Michael's brother per the tree (I2), bought land in Schuylkill County in 1875 (F4, Deed Book 42 p. 118, source S1), seven years before Michael's move. If Patrick was already there, he may be the pull behind Michael's move. The seller, James Kelly, and the deeds next to Patrick's entry may show other Sheahans or associates from the same home place. Browse the Deed Book 42 entry and the grantor index for Kelly and Sheahan for 1875-1885. The census item for Patrick is part of the census plan item above.

Local newspaper notices from the coal region for 1880-1883 may report mine openings, hiring drives, or strikes that drew workers in, and may name Michael or Patrick. No indexed Schuylkill newspaper collection appears in the locality survey, so this item has to be located through the FamilySearch catalog or a state or county repository before it can be searched. It tests the work-driven explanation (the family tradition) directly, which the other items do not.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Question: q_001, "Who were the parents of Alan Glen Applegarth (b. 29 Apr 1936, Ogden, Weber County, Utah)?"

Survey, what the project already holds:
- The tree links Alan (I1) to John Obrien Applegarth (I2) and Olive Annie Harvey (I3) as parents, citing the 1940 census (S1), the Weber County marriage record (S3) and a 2023 obituary (S4).
- The 1940 census (log_001, Ada County, Idaho) and the 1950 census (log_002, Ogden) both show John O. and Olive with son Alan.
- The 20 Oct 1926 Weber County marriage of John Obrien Applegarth and Olive Annie Harvey (log_003) is an indexed hit that also gives the mother's maiden name.
- The 2023 obituary (log_005) names the parents John O. and Olive Harvey Applegarth.
- Church and LDS records (log_006) and Weber County probate for 1970-1998 (log_007) were searched with no result.

Plan items, in order:
1. pli_001, vital record, Utah state registration, 1936 birth. Names both parents directly. Access is restricted, so eligibility needs confirming.
2. pli_002, vital record, 1926 Weber County marriage, checked against the original image on FamilySearch. This is the dedicated parents'-marriage item.
3. pli_003, vital record, any marriage of Olive Annie before 1926, 1915-1926. Tests whether Harvey is her birth surname or a prior married name.
4. pli_004, vital record, Olive Annie Harvey's birth or baptism, 1890-1915, to name her parents. The window is an estimate because the project has no birth year for her.
5. pli_005, census, FAN item: the Harvey household in the 1940 census, Weber County, indexed on FamilySearch.
6. pli_006, newspaper, Ogden obituaries of Olive (d. 1970) and John O. (d. 1998), listing surviving children.
7. pli_007, vital record, Alan's 2023 death certificate, Cache County. Required because he has died. It may be restricted.

No fallback relationships are set. Nothing in this plan is a conclusion, and the question still needs research-exhaustiveness before proof. Items 2 to 5 are FamilySearch searches, so the next step is search-records. Items 1, 6 and 7 may need access steps outside FamilySearch.

I set up a plan of seven searches to settle who Alan Glen Applegarth's parents were. Much of the evidence already points to John Obrien Applegarth and Olive Annie Harvey: the 1940 and 1950 censuses, their 1926 marriage, and a 2023 obituary. The plan checks the marriage against the original image, looks for any earlier marriage of Olive, and searches for a birth record for Alan and for Olive's own parents. It also covers her sibling household in the 1940 census, the parents' obituaries, and Alan's death certificate.

The next step is to run the FamilySearch searches in this plan, starting with the marriage image check.

The 20 Oct 1926 marriage of John Obrien Applegarth and Olive Annie Harvey (log_003, src_003) is known so far only from an indexed entry. Checking the original county marriage image confirms the couple as a unit and the bride's name as written, and fixes the date that places Alan's birth after the marriage. items.jurisdiction: Utah, Weber County first, then adjoining Utah counties
items.rationale: Companion to the 1926 marriage: the project knows Olive Annie only as Harvey from that one marriage and her 1950 household. Searching for any marriage of Olive Annie before 1926 tests whether Harvey is her birth surname or a prior married name. Her remarriage, if any, would change which marriage record names her parents.

Olive Annie Harvey's own birth or baptism record would name her parents, which tests the Harvey line and identifies Olive as the daughter of a known couple. The project has no birth year for her, so this window is an estimate and should be narrowed once her age at the 1926 marriage or her death record is read.

FAN item: the Harvey household in the 1940 census, which the locality entry marks as indexed with relationship to head. Siblings and parents of Olive Annie listed there would confirm her parentage and identify a relative who may hold family records. Search the Harvey surname with Olive's given names as a check of the household.

Obituaries of Olive Annie (died 1970) and John O. Applegarth (died 1998) would list surviving children and sometimes birthplaces, which corroborates Alan as their son and tests the parent-child link from a source written close to each death. No probate naming the children was found (log_007), so obituaries are the next test. Obituaries of this period are usually held on microfilm or in newspaper archives, so confirm access.

Alan died in 2023, per the GenealogyBank obituary (src_004, place Cache County). His death certificate would name his parents with the informant's knowledge, giving a record with a different source chain from the census and marriage evidence. Utah restricts recent death certificates to eligible requesters, so this item may end in a restricted or unavailable result.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn is about 35 here. The tree holds Patrick as born about 1845 in Ireland and Thomas Flynn as born about 1818 in Ireland, and the 1860 census entry in the log placed Patrick aged 15 in Thomas's Schuylkill household. The 1880 census is the first federal census with a relationship-to-head column, and it records each person's father's and mother's birthplace. It therefore tests whether Thomas (about 62) is listed as Patrick's father in a household, and whether Patrick's own entry says Ireland, which conflicts with the death certificate's Pennsylvania (a secondary statement by the son-in-law informant). Name-searchable. Identity check: only a Thomas Flynn of about the right age with an Irish birthplace in Schuylkill is accepted as the same man.

Patrick is alive here (the death certificate gives his death as 12 March 1908) at about 55. The 1900 census gives relationship to head, birth month and year, and each person's parents' birthplaces. It can show Patrick as head of his own household, as a son in Thomas's household if Thomas (about 82) is still living, or as a member of a child's household, and it names the wife. The parents' birthplace entries are a direct test of the Ireland claim against the death certificate's Pennsylvania. Name-searchable.

Patrick is about 25 and Thomas about 52 in this census, the first after the 1860 entry that placed Patrick in Thomas's household. The 1870 census names every person but gives no relationship column and no parents' birthplaces, so co-residence with a Thomas Flynn of Irish birth can be shown, but a son relationship cannot be read from it. It tests whether Patrick had left the household by 1870. Name-searchable. Schuylkill County was formed in 1811, so no boundary change affects this search.

Fan item, required on a parentage question. James Brown gave the 1908 death certificate and is named there as Patrick's son-in-law, so he married one of Patrick's daughters; that daughter's name is not in the tree. Brown's household in 1900 may hold Patrick or Patrick's wife as a co-resident, and the entry for his wife's parents' birthplace or her own birth details may name Patrick's Irish or Pennsylvania origin. Search James Brown in Schuylkill with a birth-year window of about 1840 to 1875 and read the household for an older Flynn. Name-searchable, and the search will return many James Browns, so the candidate must be tied to a Flynn in the same household.

Fallback for the 1880 Schuylkill search. If Patrick is not in Schuylkill in 1880, he may have moved within Pennsylvania, and the same Irish-born Patrick and the same Thomas would be found in the statewide index. Name-searchable. Accept a match only where the birthplace and the age fit the Patrick known from the tree.
Fallback for the 1900 Schuylkill search. If Patrick is not in Schuylkill in 1900, a statewide search for the Irish-born Patrick of about 1845 can locate a move. Name-searchable.
Fallback for the 1870 Schuylkill search. If Patrick or Thomas is not in Schuylkill in 1870, a statewide search will test whether the household moved. Name-searchable.

Parentage item for the candidate couple, Thomas Flynn and his wife, whose marriage would fall in the years before Patrick's birth about 1845. The marriage record can supply the mother's name if this was Thomas's first marriage, and the 1870 to 1900 census entries may name her as wife. ## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

The orphans' court records include marriages (since 1885), births and deaths (1893-1905) and adoptions (since 1925), besides estate dockets and distributions.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.question: Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?
items.rationale: This is the primary research objective.

items.exhaustive_search_summary: Searched 1850 census (FamilySearch, Ancestry, MyHeritage — log_001, log_002, log_003), 1860 census (FamilySearch — log_004), and death certificate (FamilySearch — log_005). 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses and Thomas Flynn's probate records not yet searched — these are the primary remaining gaps.
items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

The parents probably married in Ireland, which the Pennsylvania locality does not cover, so this item may return nothing. A separate Irish-origin marriage item needs a locality survey for Ireland first. The Pennsylvania county marriage collection is name-searchable.

Patrick's burial, the subject's own death entry (the death certificate, pli_005, is already searched). A burial record may give his age, birthplace or parents' names. The Pennsylvania cemetery records collection is name-searchable.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.guide_markdown:
## Muhlenberg County, Kentucky — c. 1870-1890

Statewide death certificates begin 1911; no certificate can cover a death in the 1870s-1880s. County death registers (1804888) exist but the 1860s-1870s coverage is partial. For this era, **probate records are the primary death evidence**: administrator bonds name the widow or heir, estate settlements are dated, and register entries bracket the death within months. Muhlenberg County probate (1875188) survives well for the 1870s and is browse-only. Supplement with church burials, cemetery records, and census bracketing.

entry.rationale: Review pending FamilySearch hints on ZZWK-EL1 before searching; an attached hint may already answer the question.

Kentucky, Deaths and Burials, 1843-1970 (collection 1804888) is name-searchable and includes county death registers for 1852-1910, the only death-record series that can cover a death between the last residence fact (1870, Muhlenberg County) and 1910. Coverage for the 1860s-1870s is partial, so a negative name search does not close the question; item 3 browses the register pages directly. Search under Wilkins and its spelling variants within the county and window.

The Muhlenberg county death register image group (1852-1910) is browse-only and almost wholly unindexed, so the register must be read page by page for an entry for Elijah Wilkins, aged roughly 56 to 76 in the 1870s-1880s. Use it as the fallback where item 2's name search finds nothing, because the register is gappy for the 1860s-1870s and a missing page is not proof of absence.

The 1870 household is the last residence fact in the tree. An 1880 enumeration in Muhlenberg County either places him alive, which moves the death window forward, or shows him absent, which brackets it between 1870 and 1880. The catalog check did not return an 1880 census collection for Kentucky, so confirm its availability before searching. Census is not a death record and cannot state a date of death.

Pre-1911 death evidence in Kentucky is probate: administrator bonds name the widow or adult son and estate settlements are dated, bracketing the death within months and localizing it to the county. The Muhlenberg probate image group (1858-1889) is browse-only with no indexed names, so read the administrator bond and settlement volumes for Elijah Wilkins's estate. Kentucky Probate Records, 1727-1990 (collection 1875188) is the same material and is browse-only.

FAN item, dependent on items 4 and 5: the 1870 and 1880 neighbours of the Wilkins household are not yet named in the project tree. Once they are identified, read the same Muhlenberg probate volumes for estate papers of those neighbours that name Elijah Wilkins as a bondsman, appraiser, purchaser at sale or creditor, since these may place him alive or dead in a dated entry. This also serves the identity part of the objective.

Church burial registers and county cemetery records can bracket the death when no death or probate entry survives, and a burial entry often gives an age or a home parish that confirms identity. No cemetery collection was returned by the catalog check, so identify the Muhlenberg churches and cemeteries from the census households before searching.

Exclusion check only. Kentucky Deaths, 1911-1967 (collection 1417491) is name-searchable, but statewide certificates begin 1 January 1911, so a death in the 1870s or 1880s cannot be in it. The search is worth running only to rule out a death after 1911, which at a birth c. 1814 would be an unusually long life. A negative result closes only the 1911-and-later window.

items.guide_markdown:
## Lincolnshire, England - 1750-1800

FamilySearch's 'England, Births and Christenings' collection (1473014) is a partial Legacy index: it does not index all records for this place or period, and no records or corrections are being added — a nil there is a statement about the index, not proof that no christening exists; search the parish register itself before concluding absence. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England,_Births_and_Christenings_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records)

entry.rationale: The project tree holds only Mary Dawson's birth as about 1772 in Lincolnshire, England, and no parents, so her baptism is the first record that can name them. Search the FamilySearch collection England, Births and Christenings, 1538-1975 (1473014), listed in the locality entry as name-searchable. That collection is a partial Legacy index, so a nil result does not prove no baptism exists and must be followed by item 2.

entry.repository: other (original parish register images at the county record office, located through the FamilySearch Catalog)
entry.rationale: Fallback for item 1. The locality entry says the FamilySearch index omits records for this place and period and is not being corrected, so the original Lincolnshire baptism registers for 1770-1775 must be read directly before concluding that no baptism exists. The parish is not yet known and is set by where the family appears later.

FAN item, required on a parentage question. Search the same baptism collection for other Dawson children, and for the godparents of any Dawson baptism in Lincolnshire, from 1760 to 1790. A sibling's baptism names the same parents, and godparents often are kin, so either can show who Mary's parents were.

Mary's own marriage record, as a lead to her origin. Marriage entries often state a parish of residence and sometimes a father's name. Her marriage may also be her only record that names her parents, and it is the source for the surname she was married under. Search the same collection, then the original register if nothing is found.

Separate item for the parents' marriage, which can only be searched once a candidate father is named by items 1 to 4. It supplies the mother's maiden name, which the baptism may omit, and it corroborates a father whose link comes only from indirect evidence. It does not by itself show that Mary is their child, so a baptism or family record must still place her with them.

entry.repository: other (England probate records at the county archives and The National Archives)
entry.rationale: A parent of a child born about 1772 would plausibly die between about 1772 and about 1830, so this window is set by the parent's lifespan, not by Mary's. A will or administration could name Mary as a daughter. It is planned after items 1 to 3 so that the candidate parents' names are known.

items.guide_markdown:
## Württemberg, Germany - 1780-1830

Her first marriage most likely falls in her late teens to twenties, so 1765-1800 is the window. Meland is a sokn of Hamre prestegjeld, so its marriages are in the Hamre church books per the locality entry. Search Unna in her spelling variants and the patronymic as Halsteinsdatter, Halstensdatter or abbreviated d./dtr., since recorders set spellings. Fallback for item 1: if the indexed marriage search finds no Unna, browse the Hamre marriage volumes for 1765-1800 page by page for the Meland entries. A sibling's marriage entry names the parents and often a witness or bondsman, who may be the husband or his kin. Look for the Halstein household's surname and the Hestdal farm name, which the locality entry names as the place-level residence, not as a surname. Name-searchable per the locality entry.

items.rationale: Search the Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926 collection for a bride named Unna Halsteinsdatter, born May 1745 at Hestdal in Meland. Her first marriage most likely falls in her late teens to twenties, so 1765-1800 is the window. Meland is a sokn of Hamre prestegjeld, so its marriages are in the Hamre church books per the locality entry. Search Unna in her spelling variants and the patronymic as Halsteinsdatter, Halstensdatter or abbreviated d./dtr., since recorders set spellings. A register entry names the groom and the date, which answers the question directly. Name-searchable per the locality entry.

Fallback for item 1: if the indexed marriage search finds no Unna, browse the Hamre marriage volumes for 1765-1800 page by page for the Meland entries. Indexing of Norwegian registers is partial and spelling is unreliable, so an image browse can catch an entry the index misses. Browse-only, so this is an image browse rather than a name search.

Search the Norway Baptisms, 1634-1927 collection for children baptised to a mother named Unna Halsteinsdatter after her marriage. A baptism names the father, so it identifies the husband even if the marriage entry is missed, and it dates the union by the first child's birth. Search the same spelling variants as item 1. Name-searchable per the locality entry.

Identity check: find Unna's own baptism in the Hamre baptisms for 1744-1746, where her father is named. Her patronymic Halsteinsdatter means daughter of Halstein, so a baptism naming Halstein as father at Hestdal confirms the right Unna before any marriage is tied to her. Without it, a marriage to a common name could be a different woman. Name-searchable per the locality entry.

FAN search: marriages in the same Hamre register of Unna's siblings, and of other Hestdal kin named as her father Halstein's family. A sibling's marriage entry names the parents and often a witness or bondsman, who may be the husband or his kin. Look for the Halstein household's surname and the Hestdal farm name, which the locality entry names as the place-level residence, not as a surname. Name-searchable per the locality entry.

Check for a household: if Unna married before 1801, the 1801 census should show her with her husband and children at Hestdal or nearby in Meland. A household listing gives relationship to head and confirms a couple living together, which the marriage entry alone does not. This is a national census not covered by the locality entry, so confirm its availability before relying on it.

Facts from the survey that bear on the question:
- The tree gives Patrick's birth as about 1845 in Ireland, and his death as 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County. The death fact cites the Pennsylvania death certificate (S3), but no assertion has been extracted from it. The objective's "born in Pennsylvania" conflicts with the tree and the 1850 census, which both say Ireland.
- The tree lists Thomas Flynn (about 1818, Ireland) as Patrick's father. That link rests on the 1850 census, where Patrick, age 5, is in Thomas's household at dwelling 84. The 1850 census states no relationships, so the child-of-head link is inferred. The mother is not yet named anywhere.
- The Ancestry index confirms that 1850 household. MyHeritage returned nothing.
- The tree cites the 1860 census (S2), but the log has no search of it.

Plan items, in execution order:
1. `pli_004`, 1908 death entry for Patrick (vital record, FamilySearch images). Pennsylvania death certificates of that date name the decedent's parents, so this could name Thomas and give the mother's maiden name. Open the certificate image, not just the index.
2. `pli_005`, 1850 census re-read of Thomas's full household, plus the neighbouring dwellings for kin (census). This is the FAN item for the parentage test. The wife was never recorded.
3. `pli_006`, 1860 and 1870 censuses for Thomas's household (census).

8. `pli_011`, Patrick's own 1908–1909 probate (probate, browse-only). Heirs could name siblings.
9. `pli_012`, 1880 census (census). It gives relationship to head and the parents' birthplaces.

Not planned: an Irish baptism or civil search. There is no locality survey for Ireland, so that needs one first. The Schuylkill locality entry carries the county-level collections.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.
